Free calm & grounding tools

20 short exercises on calm & grounding, 2 to 8 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • Five senses grounding

    Five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste. A way back into the room when your mind has left it.

    Guided exercise · 4 min

  • Tense and release

    Work through the body tightening each muscle group for a few seconds and then letting go. Many people do not notice how much they are holding until they let it drop.

    Guided exercise · 8 min

  • Coherent breathing

    Five seconds in, five seconds out, no holds. A steady, even rhythm many people find easiest to keep up for a few minutes at a time.

    Breathing · 4 min

  • The long exhale

    Four seconds in, eight seconds out, no holds. Making the out-breath twice as long as the in-breath is one of the simplest ways many people find to settle a body that is running fast.

    Breathing · 3 min

  • The double breath

    Two breaths in through the nose, the second one a small top-up, then one long breath out through the mouth. The shape of a sigh, done deliberately, a handful of times.

    Breathing · 2 min

  • The humming breath

    Breathe in through the nose, then hum the whole way out. The vibration in the chest and face gives the mind something to rest on, and the hum stretches the out-breath without any counting.

    Breathing · 3 min

  • The cold water reset

    A guided minute with cold water on the face, the wrists, or the back of the neck. A fast, physical way many people use to interrupt a spiral when breathing alone is not reaching it.

    Guided exercise · 4 min

  • A slow walk, felt from the feet

    Five minutes of walking slower than feels natural, with attention kept in the soles of the feet. Grounding that uses the whole body, for people who cannot sit still to calm down.

    Guided exercise · 7 min

  • What gets between you and calm

    Sort the things that keep you from settling by how much say you have over them. Some of what makes life loud can be turned down; some can only be worked around, and it helps to know which is which.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • How you know you are settling

    Choose the signs your body gives when calm starts to arrive. Most people know their signs for stress in detail and their signs for settling not at all, which makes the calm easy to miss.

    Card pick · 4 min

  • Where you are right now, on six dials

    A one-minute check-in on the state you are in at this moment: the breath, the muscles, the speed of thought, and how much of the room you can feel. Useful before and after anything meant to settle you.

    Dials · 2 min

  • How you relate to quiet

    Rate how often a set of habits around stillness has been true for you lately. For some people calm is a relief; for others it is a gap that has to be filled fast, and it helps to know which you are.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Signs your body is on alert

    Tick the small ways a body shows it has not fully stood down: the startle, the scanning, the jaw. These are the habits grounding is meant to loosen, and the first step is knowing yours.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • A memory of calm, in detail

    Write your way back into one moment when you felt fully at ease, sense by sense, until you can find the part of it you could bring into the room you are in now.

    Guided writing · 7 min

  • Seven days of settling

    Each evening, rate how settled you felt overall, how much you moved your body, and how much of the day was spent off a screen. After a week the three lines start to explain each other.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • Design a calm corner

    Plan one small spot at home, or wherever you spend your days, that is set up for settling: where it is, what is in it, what is kept out, and the signal that tells you it is time to use it.

    Plan builder · 6 min

  • Things people believe about calm

    Turn over cards that show a common belief about being calm on one side and a more forgiving angle on the back. A lot of what makes calm hard to reach is the idea of what it is supposed to look like.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • Soothing or numbing

    Place the things you reach for when you need to feel better on a grid of how often you reach for them against how you actually feel afterwards. Both corners feel like calm in the moment; only one still does an hour later.

    Grid · 6 min

  • Your grounding order

    Rank a set of grounding moves from the one you trust most to the one you trust least. Everybody's order is different, and knowing yours means you do not have to think when it is loud.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • When you feel most settled

    Mark the times in a typical week when you feel most at ease. Most week maps track the trouble; this one maps the calm, so you can see where it already lives and put more next to it.

    Week map · 3 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
